claims.text: A stable surface passivation layer governs structural and chemical stability in initially single-phase, near-equiatomic five-metal nanoparticles.
Surface passivation reduces high-temperature surface diffusion of reactive elements.
Passivated nanoparticles retain a single-phase, near-equiatomic composition from 473 K through 1923 K.
Unpassivated nanoparticles undergo surface-mediated segregation at elevated temperatures.
Unpassivated samples eventually undergo phase decomposition at elevated temperatures.
The initial material consists of single-phase, near-equiatomic five-metal nanoparticles with a uniform elemental distribution.
A stable surface passivation layer can suppress selective oxidation of more reactive species.
A stable surface passivation layer can suppress segregation of more reactive species.
Passivation chemically stabilizes the local atomic environment.
Chemical stabilization by passivation reduces the driving force for surface diffusion.
Reduced surface diffusion minimizes the growth of composition gradients and second-phase precipitates at high temperature.
Relative to unpassivated controls, passivated nanoparticles exhibit less elemental segregation and phase formation.
Unpassivated nanoparticles develop localized chemical fluctuations and multiple phases above approximately 1000 K.
The proposed stabilization applies only when the passivation layer remains well adhered and stable at the operating temperature.
The phase-decomposition and passivation-stability temperatures may vary with alloy composition and processing method.
Comparable segregation or decomposition in passivated and unpassivated samples would falsify the proposed passivation effect, provided the coating remained intact.
